transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, it's... I don't even know where to start, really. I guess the main thing, the reason I finally made the appointment, is that I just feel so worn down. Almost all the time. And it's not like I'm not sleeping, because I am. I try to be really good about my sleep hygiene, you know? Going to bed at the same time, making sure the room is dark, all of that. But even after a full night's sleep, I wake up and I just feel... heavy. Like my batteries are still on zero. 

And then I have to drag myself to work—I work in a lab, I'm a physical scientist, so it's a lot of focus and precision, which is hard when you're this tired. By the time I get through the day there, and then commute home, and then walk into my house... well, the house is just a whole other thing. There's always clutter everywhere, mail piling up, dishes, laundry that needs folding. I try to tackle it, I really do, but by the time I've dealt with work and just the bare minimum of keeping the house from falling apart, I have absolutely nothing left. Very little energy for anything else. I used to read, or go for walks, but now I just kind of sit there because I'm so depleted. It's just this constant, endless fatigue that I can't seem to shake, no matter what I do or how much coffee I drink.
Do you still find pleasure in activities that you used to enjoy, like reading?

Well, with the reading, I try to pick up a book and I just... I don't know, it doesn't hold me. But it's not just the reading. It’s really everything. Most days, there’s just this... this low, gray mood running in the background of my entire life. 

Like, I can still go to the lab, obviously. I go in, I do my work, I can talk to people by the breakroom and smile and pretend everything is fine, and I'm sure none of my colleagues even notice anything is off. I'm still doing what I need to do to get by. But inside, I just don't really feel light or excited about much of anything anymore. 

For example, I used to be so passionate about baking. I would spend whole weekends proofing bread, getting the hydration percentages exactly right—which is very satisfying for a physical scientist, you know, getting all the variables perfectly balanced and watching the reaction. I used to love the whole process of it. But now, I can't even be bothered to pull the flour out of the pantry. And my telescope, too. I have this really nice telescope set up by the back window, and I used to love checking it on clear nights, looking at the craters on the moon or trying to spot Jupiter's moons. It was genuinely thrilling to me. Now, I just walk right past it. It's just sitting there gathering dust and I feel... nothing. I just don't have that spark for it. It's like everything is just kind of overshadowed by that gray feeling I mentioned, so even if I have the time to do something I used to enjoy, the actual enjoyment just isn't there to meet me.
Do you still feel pleasure when you are doing something that you used to enjoy, even if you don't feel like doing it?

Well, that's the thing, isn't it? Even if I force myself to do it... like, say I actually drag myself into the kitchen on a Sunday afternoon. I wipe down the counters, I get out the digital scale, I measure out the bread flour and the water and the starter. I go through all the physical motions that used to bring me so much satisfaction, right? The kneading, the waiting, the folding. And I'm standing there, doing it, and I'm just waiting for that familiar feeling to kick in. That sense of accomplishment or just... quiet joy, I guess. But it just doesn't come. 

It's like I'm going through a script that someone else wrote for me. I can bake the bread perfectly, and it comes out of the oven looking beautiful, smelling great, and I just look at it and feel... empty. There's no payoff. And it's the same with the telescope. A couple of weeks ago, there was a really clear night, perfect seeing conditions, no humidity. I forced myself to calibrate the finder scope, got everything aligned, looked through the eyepiece... and it was just a rock in the sky. I didn't feel any of that awe I used to feel. So, no, even when I push through and actually do the things, the pleasure just isn't there anymore. It's incredibly frustrating because I know I *should* be enjoying it, but my brain just won't cooperate.
Do you often feel guilty about anything?

Guilty? Um... no, I don't think so. I mean, not in any sort of big, overwhelming way. Like, I don't sit around agonizing over past mistakes or feeling like I'm a terrible person or anything like that. I know some people get really bogged down in regret or feel like they're a burden to everyone around them, but that's not really what's happening with me. 

I guess... I mean, sure, I feel a little bad sometimes when I look at the state of the house, like I mentioned before. The mail on the counter, the laundry... I'll look at it and think, "I really should have handled that by now, an adult should be able to keep their living space tidy." Or maybe a passing twinge of guilt if I haven't called my mom back right away because I just don't have the energy to talk. But it's not this deep, gnawing guilt, you know? It's more just... annoyance at myself for being so tired. It's not like I feel guilty for existing or for things that aren't my fault. It's just the normal, everyday stuff, but even then, it's mostly just overshadowed by how exhausted and flat I feel. So, no, guilt isn't really a major part of this for me.
Do you find yourself moving or speaking more slowly than you used to?

Moving or speaking more slowly? Um... no, I haven't really noticed anything like that. I mean, I still get around the lab at the same pace, I think. I'm definitely tired, like I said, and sometimes getting out of bed feels like I'm moving through molasses, just because the motivation isn't there. But once I'm actually up and moving, my physical speed is pretty normal. 

I don't think my speech has slowed down either. I mean, you can probably tell I still talk plenty. When I'm explaining a procedure to one of the junior techs or giving an update at our weekly meetings, I'm pretty sure I sound exactly the same as I always have. I'm still articulate, I can still get my point across without trailing off or taking huge pauses to find my words. It's not like my brain is working slower, it's just... the emotional register is turned down. 

So, yeah, physically, I'm functioning fine. I'm not shuffling down the hallways or taking five minutes to answer a simple question. It's all internal. The machinery is still running at the normal speed, it's just the battery that feels completely drained, if that makes sense. But no, no actual slowness in how I move or talk.
Do you often feel worthless?

Worthless? No, I wouldn't say that. I mean, I know I'm good at my job. I've been at the lab for over a decade now, and they rely on me. When there's a tricky calibration issue with the mass spectrometer, they come to me. I know I have value in that sense, as a professional, as a scientist. I have skills that took years to develop, and I'm competent. I don't sit around thinking I'm a waste of space or that I have nothing to offer the world. 

It's more just... a feeling of pointlessness, I guess? Which isn't the same as worthlessness. Like, I know *I* have worth, but I sometimes wonder what the worth of *doing* anything is. Like with the bread or the telescope. I know I'm capable of making the sourdough, I know I'm a good baker, I know I'm smart enough to track a celestial object. My worth isn't in question. It's just... why bother if it doesn't make me feel anything? 

So, no, I don't look in the mirror and think, "You're useless" or "You're worthless." I know my friends care about me, even if I haven't been the most attentive friend lately. I know my mom loves me. I know my colleagues respect me. I just... I feel like a perfectly functional, valuable machine that's just been unplugged from whatever power source makes life actually feel vibrant. I have worth, I just don't have... joy. So, no, worthlessness isn't really one of the things I'm dealing with. I just feel incredibly, persistently flat.
Have you noticed any changes in your appetite?

Appetite? Um, no, I don't think there's been any real change there. I mean, I still eat three meals a day, pretty much like clockwork. I've always been a bit of a creature of habit when it comes to food. Like, for breakfast, it's usually just a bowl of oatmeal with some berries, maybe a little almond butter stirred in. And I still eat that every morning before I head to the lab. I haven't noticed myself skipping it or anything. 

And lunch is usually just whatever I packed the night before, usually leftovers or a turkey sandwich. I still eat it at my desk while I'm reviewing data, just like I always have. I'm not, you know, ravenous or anything, but I'm not skipping meals either. I haven't noticed my clothes fitting any differently, so I don't think I've gained or lost any significant amount of weight. 

I guess the only thing is... maybe the food just doesn't taste quite as exciting as it used to? Like, I used to really look forward to trying a new recipe on the weekends, or going out to that Thai place near my apartment. Now, it's more just about fueling the machine, you know? I eat because I know I need to, because if I don't, I'll get a headache or my blood sugar will drop and I won't be able to concentrate on my work. But I'm not sitting around craving things or losing my appetite completely. It's just... routine. Exactly the same routine it's always been, just maybe lacking a little bit of the enjoyment I used to get from a really good meal. But as far as the actual amount I'm eating, or feeling hungry? No, that's all stayed pretty much exactly the same.
Have you had any thoughts about not wanting to be alive?

Thoughts about not wanting to be alive? Oh, no. No, definitely not. I know it can sound like that, when I talk about everything feeling so flat and pointless, and how I'm just kind of going through the motions every day, but it's not that I want to die or anything. I don't have any thoughts of hurting myself or ending my life. 

It's more like... I just wish I could feel more *alive* while I'm here. Like I was saying about the sourdough or the telescope, I just want that spark back. I want to care about things the way I used to. But I don't want to stop existing. I still have my job, which I'm good at, and my mom, and my friends... even if I'm not the best at keeping in touch right now. 

I think about the future sometimes, you know? Like, what I'm going to do when I retire, or if I'll ever get around to publishing that paper on the isotopic variations I've been tracking for the last three years. I have plans, I have things I need to do. It's just that right now, the day-to-day process of doing them feels like such a chore. It's like I'm walking on a treadmill that's turned up just a little too high, and I'm tired, but I'm not trying to jump off the machine entirely. I just want someone to lower the incline, or maybe give me a glass of water. 

So, no, I'm not suicidal. I don't sit in the dark wishing I wouldn't wake up. I just sit in the dark wishing I felt excited to wake up. Does that make sense? It's a very distinct difference in my head. I value my life, I just wish the quality of it—the emotional texture of it—was better than it is right now. But no thoughts of not wanting to be here. Not at all.
How long have you been feeling this way?

How long? Oh, wow, um... it's been a while. It's not like it happened overnight, you know? It wasn't like waking up one Tuesday and suddenly everything was gray. It was more insidious than that, just this slow, creeping sort of dullness that just settled over everything. But if I really trace it back, if I really think about when I stopped feeling like myself and started feeling like this... this version of me that just operates on autopilot... I'd say it's been a little over two years. 

Yeah, definitely over two years now, because it started shortly after we moved into the older house. We had been looking for a place for so long, and I thought getting out of the apartment and having a real house with a yard and a proper kitchen for baking would change things, maybe give me a boost. But almost as soon as we got the boxes unpacked—well, most of the boxes, there are still a few in the guest room that I just haven't had the energy to deal with—that's when this low baseline really established itself. 

I remember it was late fall, right around the time the leaves were all gone and the trees were just bare branches, and I was standing in this new, bigger kitchen that I'd wanted so badly, looking out the window, and I just felt... nothing. No excitement about the new house, no motivation to paint the walls or set up my telescope on the new patio. Just this heavy, persistent flatness. And it hasn't lifted since. It's just been this constant, low-level hum of apathy for over twenty-four months now. Every season, every holiday, every project at the lab... just the same flat line. So, yeah, a little over two years of just... existing like this.
Have you noticed yourself fidgeting or feeling restless more often than usual?

Fidgeting? Restless? Um, no, not really. I mean, I'm not bouncing my leg under the desk or pacing around the lab or anything like that. If anything, it's almost the opposite, you know? Like I was saying about that heavy feeling, it's more like I just want to sit still. When I'm at work, I can sit in front of the mass spectrometer for hours just running samples and reviewing the readouts, and I don't feel this urge to get up and move around. I just sit there. 

And at home, it's the same thing. I'll sit on the couch after dinner—usually just watching some documentary or a show I've already seen a dozen times because I don't have the mental energy to follow a new plot—and I just stay there until it's time to go to bed. I'm not restless at all. I don't have that nervous energy where you feel like you need to be doing something with your hands or walking around the block. I mean, my mom is like that, she's always knitting or cleaning something, she can't just sit and watch a movie without doing something else at the same time. But I've never really been like that, and definitely not lately. 

I guess the only time I move around a lot is when I'm actually setting up an experiment, but that's just the physical requirement of the job, moving beakers and adjusting the equipment. It's purposeful movement, not restlessness. When I don't have a specific task to do, I'm perfectly content—well, maybe content isn't the right word, but I'm perfectly inclined to just be completely still. So no, no fidgeting or feeling like I can't sit still. It's really just the opposite. I just feel very... stationary.
Do you think your movements or reactions have slowed down compared to how they used to be?

Slowed down? Um... you know, I haven't really thought about it like that. I don't think so? I mean, I'm not moving in slow motion or anything like that. When I'm at the lab, I still get all my work done. I can calibrate the instruments just as fast as I always have, and I don't think my colleagues are waiting on me to hand over data or anything. I haven't noticed myself physically taking longer to walk down the hall to the breakroom or, you know, taking ten minutes to put on my coat. 

I guess... well, mentally, maybe I feel a little sluggish sometimes, like it takes a bit more effort to get the gears turning when I have to write up a report or analyze a really complex data set. But physically? My reactions? No, I don't think my movements have actually slowed down. If I drop a pen, I still catch it before it hits the floor—well, most of the time, anyway. And driving, my reaction time there feels completely normal. I'm not, like, hesitating at stoplights or anything. 

It's really just that internal feeling of heaviness I mentioned before, the lack of drive to start moving in the first place. But once I am moving, once I'm actually doing a task, my speed seems pretty much the same as it was before this whole two-year slump started. So, no, I wouldn't say my movements or reactions are slower. I just... I just don't want to move as much, if that makes sense. But the actual speed of it all seems perfectly fine.
Do you feel like you're able to initiate activities as easily as you used to?

Initiate activities? Oh, no. No, definitely not. That’s actually a big part of why I’m here, honestly, because I just feel so worn down almost all the time. It’s like there’s this massive barrier to starting anything. And it’s not for lack of sleep, either, which is the really frustrating part. I can get a full night’s sleep—I’ll go to bed at a reasonable hour, sleep right through the night, wake up the next morning, and I still just feel completely exhausted before my feet even hit the floor. 

So, by the time I drag myself out of bed, get through my shift at the lab, and then come home... well, I come home to the house, and like I mentioned, there are still those unpacked boxes in the guest room, plus just the general daily clutter that piles up. The mail on the counter, the dishes, the clean laundry sitting in the basket that I haven't folded. Just handling my basic work responsibilities and trying to manage that house clutter takes absolutely everything out of me. I have very little left for anything else. 

If I think about initiating something extra, like, say, finally pulling out my baking supplies to make bread, or setting up that telescope on the patio like I originally planned when we moved... I just can't. The thought of gathering the materials, or getting the flour out, it just feels like trying to run a marathon in waist-deep mud. I used to be able to just decide to do a project and then go do it, you know? But now, because I'm just so constantly drained, the tank is completely empty by the time the bare minimum is done. So no, starting things is incredibly difficult now. I just don't have the reserves for it anymore.
Do you feel like it takes you longer to think or react to things compared to how you used to?

Thinking? Yeah, actually, that part... that part is definitely different. I know I just said my physical reactions are fine, but mentally... it's like wading through molasses sometimes. I used to be so sharp, you know? My brain would just click from one step to the next. But now, it's like my thoughts are just moving in slow motion. 

Take my work, for example. I do a lot of grant writing and revisions for the lab, and it used to be a very clean, sequential process for me. I'd read a paragraph, immediately see what needed to be tightened up, make the edits, and move on. Boom, boom, boom. But lately? I'll sit there staring at the same paragraph for twenty minutes. I'll read a sentence, and it's like the words just kind of float there, and it takes me twice as long to process what it actually means in the context of the whole proposal. And then when I go to rewrite it, I just... I get stuck. I second-guess every little word choice. Is "indicate" better than "demonstrate"? Does this sentence flow into the next one properly? I'll rewrite the same sentence four times and still not be sure if it's right. 

And it's not just at work, either. It bleeds into everything. Even something stupidly simple, like picking out materials for a home repair. The other week, I noticed the weatherstripping on the back door was peeling off, so I went to the hardware store to get a replacement. I stood in that aisle for what felt like an eternity. There were, like, three options—foam, rubber, vinyl—and I just stood there, paralyzed, trying to weigh the pros and cons of each one in my head, and my brain just felt so incredibly slow and foggy. I couldn't just make a decision. I kept going back and forth, second-guessing myself over a ten-dollar roll of tape. I ended up leaving without buying anything because it was just too much mental effort. 

So, yeah, my thinking is definitely slower. It takes me so much longer to process information and make even the smallest decisions because my mind just feels... clouded, I guess. It’s really frustrating, especially because I rely on my brain so much for my job. It’s like the processor is just running on a fraction of its normal speed.
Do you feel like your thoughts and physical movements are happening at a slower pace than they used to?

Well, like I was saying just a moment ago, it's really a split between the two. Physically? No, I don't think my movements are slower. I really don't. Like I said, I'm not moving in slow motion, I can still calibrate all my lab instruments at my normal pace, I can walk down the hall just fine, and I can catch a dropped pen. My physical reaction time, my driving, all of that feels completely normal. It's just that it takes a lot of effort to *start* moving because I'm so exhausted all the time. But the actual physical pace of my body once I'm going? That hasn't changed.

But my thoughts... yeah, that's a completely different story. Mentally, everything feels incredibly slow. Like I mentioned with the grant writing at the lab—it used to be so quick and easy for me to read a paragraph, spot the errors, and rewrite it. Boom, boom, boom. Now I just stare at it, and the words float there, and it takes me twice as long to process what I'm even looking at. And then I get completely bogged down second-guessing every single word choice. And it's not just work, it's everything. Like that time at the hardware store I just told you about, standing in the aisle for what felt like forever, completely paralyzed over which weatherstripping to buy for the back door. Foam, rubber, vinyl... I just couldn't process it or make a simple decision because my brain felt so foggy and slow. 

So, it's really frustrating. It's like my body is operating at its normal speed, but my brain is just wading through molasses. The mental processor is definitely running on a fraction of its normal speed, even though my physical movements are perfectly fine. I just... I wish my brain could keep up with my body again, you know? It’s just so draining to feel this slow mentally.
Do you feel like you have been speaking more slowly than you used to?

Speaking more slowly? Um... no, I don't think so. I mean, I know I just went on and on about how my brain feels like it's moving through molasses, and how it takes me forever to process a paragraph for a grant proposal or pick out weatherstripping, but when I'm actually talking? No, I think I speak at pretty much the exact same pace I always have. 

Actually, if anything, I might talk a little too much sometimes, like I'm doing right now, just trying to get all the details out so you understand exactly what I'm experiencing. But the actual speed of my words coming out of my mouth? No, I haven't noticed any change there. My husband hasn't said anything about me talking slower, either, and he's usually the first one to point out if I'm doing something weird or different. And at the lab, when I'm giving a presentation or just discussing a project with one of the techs, I'm pretty sure I'm talking at my normal clip. 

It's weird, right? Because you'd think if my thoughts are moving so slowly, my speech would slow down to match it. But it's almost like once I finally figure out what I want to say—once I get past all that mental fog and the second-guessing—the words just come out normally. It's the getting to the words that takes so long, not the actual speaking of them. Like, if you ask me a question, there might be a longer pause before I answer because I'm trying to formulate the thought, but once I start talking, the pace is fine. So, yeah, no, my speech speed hasn't changed at all.
Do you find it difficult to initiate or complete tasks due to feeling physically slowed down?

No, not really. I mean, like I've been saying, I don't feel physically slowed down at all. It's not my body that's the problem. I can get up, I can walk, I can move my hands... all of that is totally normal. It's the mental part that makes things hard to start or finish. 

Like, if I need to calibrate a piece of equipment in the lab, the physical act of turning the dials or pressing the buttons isn't what stops me. It's the mental energy it takes to decide to go over there and do it, and then the focus it takes to make sure I'm doing it right. Or at home... I mentioned the weatherstripping earlier. If I had actually bought the tape, physically applying it to the door wouldn't have been an issue. I have the dexterity, I have the physical speed. It was the mental hurdle of choosing the tape that stopped the whole project before it even started. 

And it's the exhaustion, too. I'm just so tired all the time. But it's a heavy, draining kind of tired, not a slow-motion kind of tired. So if I'm putting off a task, it's usually because I just don't have the energy to face it, or because my brain feels too foggy to figure out the steps, not because my body is moving too slowly to get it done. Once I actually force myself to start moving, the physical part is fine. It's just... getting over that initial wall of exhaustion and mental sludge, you know? But physically, no, I'm not moving any slower than I used to.
Do you feel like your overall activity level has decreased compared to how it used to be?

Um, overall activity level... yeah, I suppose it has decreased, but it's sort of complicated. It's not like I'm just lying in bed all day staring at the ceiling, you know? I'm still getting my lab work done. I show up, I do the physical tasks, I run the instruments. But, like I was saying before, the mental stuff—the grant drafts, the routine project decisions—those take noticeably longer now. So in a way, I'm less productive, even if I'm physically present for the same amount of time. I'm just getting less done because I get so bogged down.

But at home... yeah, that's where you really see the drop-off in my activity. I used to have all these hobbies that I really enjoyed, things that gave my downtime some structure. I used to bake a lot, you know, trying out new bread recipes on the weekends. And I had this whole bonsai collection started—which actually takes a lot of daily attention and pruning and wiring, it's quite intricate. And I had even drawn up all these plans to build a mount for my telescope so I could do some amateur astronomy in the backyard. 

But lately? I've just stopped keeping up with all of it. The bonsai trees are probably dying because I just can't bring myself to go out and tend to them. The telescope plans are just sitting in a drawer gathering dust. And baking? I can't even remember the last time I turned the oven on for something that wasn't a frozen pizza. I just come home from the lab, and I'm so utterly drained from trying to push through the mental fog all day that I just don't have the bandwidth for anything else. I end up just sitting on the couch, not really doing anything at all. So, yes, my overall activity level has definitely gone down, especially when it comes to the things I actually used to want to do. It's just... it's all too much effort now.
Do you feel like you have been experiencing any physical slowing down of your movements or reactions?

Physical slowing down? Um, no, not really. I mean, I know I've been talking a lot about how my brain feels like it's stuck in this thick sludge, and how just the thought of doing something feels impossible, but physically? No, I don't think my body is moving any slower than it used to. 

Like, if I drop a pen in the lab, I still reach out and grab it before it rolls off the table. My reflexes are fine. And when I'm walking from the parking lot to the building, I'm not shuffling or dragging my feet or anything like that. I still walk at my usual pace, which is actually pretty brisk because I'm usually running a few minutes behind schedule these days. 

It's just so frustrating because my body is perfectly capable of moving at a normal speed, but my brain just won't cooperate. It's like the engine is running fine, but the transmission is shot, you know? The signal just isn't getting through. But the actual physical movements? No, I haven't noticed any kind of slowing down there. My husband hasn't said anything about it either, and like I said, he notices everything. If I were moving like a zombie, he would have definitely pointed it out by now. So, no, physically I think I'm moving just fine. It's just everything else that feels so incredibly slow and heavy.
Do you feel like your thoughts and movements are slowed down at the same time?

No, definitely not at the same time, mostly because... well, like I was just saying a second ago, my movements aren't slowed down at all. So they can't really happen together. It's an entirely one-sided thing. 

My thoughts? Yes, absolutely. They are incredibly slow. It's like... imagine trying to do complex math in your head when you've got a terrible head cold and you've taken too much cough syrup. That's what my thought process feels like almost all day. If I'm trying to figure out the dilution ratios for a new batch of reagents in the lab, my brain is just... crawling. I'll be staring at my notebook, and it takes me three times as long to process the numbers or remember the next step in the protocol. 

But while my brain is doing that whole slow-motion routine, my body is completely fine. I might be tapping my pen against the desk at a totally normal speed, or I'll quickly reach over and grab a different beaker without any hesitation or sluggishness. There's just this huge disconnect between the two. It's honestly kind of bizarre, because you'd naturally assume that if your brain is lagging, your body would lag too, right? Like they'd be synced up somehow. But for me, it's strictly the cognitive side—the thinking, the deciding, the processing—that's stuck in the mud. The physical side of things, the actual moving of my arms and legs, that's just as quick as it ever was. So no, I wouldn't say they are both slowed down at the same time at all. It's really just my thoughts that are dragging.
Do you feel like your body movements have slowed down compared to how they used to be?

I'm sorry, I feel like we're kind of going in circles here a little bit. Didn't I just... I mean, maybe I'm not explaining it clearly enough, but like I was saying just a moment ago, no, my body movements haven't slowed down at all compared to how they used to be. They're exactly the same. 

I'm definitely not moving in slow motion or anything like that. If I'm, say, calibrating the spectrometer at work, my hands are moving just as nimbly and quickly as they did five years ago. Or even just doing mundane things, like... well, folding laundry, on the rare days I can actually muster the mental energy to get a load out of the dryer. When I'm actually doing the physical act of folding, my arms and hands are working at a perfectly normal speed. 

It's really important to me that I'm being clear about this, because I don't want to give you the wrong impression and have you write down the wrong thing. My physical body is absolutely fine, it hasn't slowed down a bit. It's strictly that mental fog I was talking about. Does that make sense? I just want to make sure I'm answering what you're actually looking for, because physically, no, there's been no change in my speed at all.

patient.answer:
Well, it's... I don't even know where to start, really. I guess the main thing, the reason I finally made the appointment, is that I just feel so worn down. Almost all the time. And it's not like I'm not sleeping, because I am. I try to be really good about my sleep hygiene, you know? Going to bed at the same time, making sure the room is dark, all of that. But even after a full night's sleep, I wake up and I just feel... heavy. Like my batteries are still on zero. 

And then I have to drag myself to work—I work in a lab, I'm a physical scientist, so it's a lot of focus and precision, which is hard when you're this tired. By the time I get through the day there, and then commute home, and then walk into my house... well, the house is just a whole other thing. There's always clutter everywhere, mail piling up, dishes, laundry that needs folding. I try to tackle it, I really do, but by the time I've dealt with work and just the bare minimum of keeping the house from falling apart, I have absolutely nothing left. Very little energy for anything else. I used to read, or go for walks, but now I just kind of sit there because I'm so depleted. It's just this constant, endless fatigue that I can't seem to shake, no matter what I do or how much coffee I drink.

patient.answer:
Well, with the reading, I try to pick up a book and I just... I don't know, it doesn't hold me. But it's not just the reading. It’s really everything. Most days, there’s just this... this low, gray mood running in the background of my entire life. 

Like, I can still go to the lab, obviously. I go in, I do my work, I can talk to people by the breakroom and smile and pretend everything is fine, and I'm sure none of my colleagues even notice anything is off. I'm still doing what I need to do to get by. But inside, I just don't really feel light or excited about much of anything anymore. 

For example, I used to be so passionate about baking. I would spend whole weekends proofing bread, getting the hydration percentages exactly right—which is very satisfying for a physical scientist, you know, getting all the variables perfectly balanced and watching the reaction. I used to love the whole process of it. But now, I can't even be bothered to pull the flour out of the pantry. And my telescope, too. I have this really nice telescope set up by the back window, and I used to love checking it on clear nights, looking at the craters on the moon or trying to spot Jupiter's moons. It was genuinely thrilling to me. Now, I just walk right past it. It's just sitting there gathering dust and I feel... nothing. I just don't have that spark for it. It's like everything is just kind of overshadowed by that gray feeling I mentioned, so even if I have the time to do something I used to enjoy, the actual enjoyment just isn't there to meet me.

And I'm standing there, doing it, and I'm just waiting for that familiar feeling to kick in. That sense of accomplishment or just... quiet joy, I guess. But it just doesn't come. 

It's like I'm going through a script that someone else wrote for me. I can bake the bread perfectly, and it comes out of the oven looking beautiful, smelling great, and I just look at it and feel... empty. There's no payoff. And it's the same with the telescope. A couple of weeks ago, there was a really clear night, perfect seeing conditions, no humidity. I forced myself to calibrate the finder scope, got everything aligned, looked through the eyepiece... and it was just a rock in the sky. I didn't feel any of that awe I used to feel. So, no, even when I push through and actually do the things, the pleasure just isn't there anymore. It's incredibly frustrating because I know I *should* be enjoying it, but my brain just won't cooperate.

Or maybe a passing twinge of guilt if I haven't called my mom back right away because I just don't have the energy to talk. But it's not this deep, gnawing guilt, you know? It's more just... annoyance at myself for being so tired. It's not like I feel guilty for existing or for things that aren't my fault. doctor.intent: Determine the presence of worthlessness

patient.answer:
Worthless? No, I wouldn't say that. I mean, I know I'm good at my job. I've been at the lab for over a decade now, and they rely on me. When there's a tricky calibration issue with the mass spectrometer, they come to me. I know I have value in that sense, as a professional, as a scientist. I have skills that took years to develop, and I'm competent. I don't sit around thinking I'm a waste of space or that I have nothing to offer the world. 

It's more just... a feeling of pointlessness, I guess? Which isn't the same as worthlessness. Like, I know *I* have worth, but I sometimes wonder what the worth of *doing* anything is. Like with the bread or the telescope. I know I'm capable of making the sourdough, I know I'm a good baker, I know I'm smart enough to track a celestial object. My worth isn't in question. It's just... why bother if it doesn't make me feel anything? 

So, no, I don't look in the mirror and think, "You're useless" or "You're worthless." I know my friends care about me, even if I haven't been the most attentive friend lately. I know my mom loves me. I know my colleagues respect me. I just... I feel like a perfectly functional, valuable machine that's just been unplugged from whatever power source makes life actually feel vibrant. I have worth, I just don't have... joy. So, no, worthlessness isn't really one of the things I'm dealing with. I just feel incredibly, persistently flat.

And I still eat that every morning before I head to the lab. I haven't noticed myself skipping it or anything. 

And lunch is usually just whatever I packed the night before, usually leftovers or a turkey sandwich. I still eat it at my desk while I'm reviewing data, just like I always have. I'm not, you know, ravenous or anything, but I'm not skipping meals either. I haven't noticed my clothes fitting any differently, so I don't think I've gained or lost any significant amount of weight. 

I guess the only thing is... maybe the food just doesn't taste quite as exciting as it used to? Like, I used to really look forward to trying a new recipe on the weekends, or going out to that Thai place near my apartment. Now, it's more just about fueling the machine, you know? I eat because I know I need to, because if I don't, I'll get a headache or my blood sugar will drop and I won't be able to concentrate on my work. But I'm not sitting around craving things or losing my appetite completely. It's just... routine. Exactly the same routine it's always been, just maybe lacking a little bit of the enjoyment I used to get from a really good meal. But as far as the actual amount I'm eating, or feeling hungry? No, that's all stayed pretty much exactly the same.

How long? Oh, wow, um... it's been a while. It's not like it happened overnight, you know? It wasn't like waking up one Tuesday and suddenly everything was gray. But if I really trace it back, if I really think about when I stopped feeling like myself and started feeling like this... this version of me that just operates on autopilot... Yeah, definitely over two years now, because it started shortly after we moved into the older house. We had been looking for a place for so long, and I thought getting out of the apartment and having a real house with a yard and a proper kitchen for baking would change things, maybe give me a boost. But almost as soon as we got the boxes unpacked—well, most of the boxes, there are still a few in the guest room that I just haven't had the energy to deal with—that's when this low baseline really established itself. 

I remember it was late fall, right around the time the leaves were all gone and the trees were just bare branches, and I was standing in this new, bigger kitchen that I'd wanted so badly, looking out the window, and I just felt... nothing. No excitement about the new house, no motivation to paint the walls or set up my telescope on the new patio. Just this heavy, persistent flatness. And it hasn't lifted since. It's just been this constant, low-level hum of apathy for over twenty-four months now. Every season, every holiday, every project at the lab... just the same flat line. So, yeah, a little over two years of just... existing like this.

target_item.name: Diminished_Thinking

patient.answer:
Thinking? Yeah, actually, that part... that part is definitely different. I know I just said my physical reactions are fine, but mentally... it's like wading through molasses sometimes. I used to be so sharp, you know? My brain would just click from one step to the next. But now, it's like my thoughts are just moving in slow motion. 

Take my work, for example. I do a lot of grant writing and revisions for the lab, and it used to be a very clean, sequential process for me. I'd read a paragraph, immediately see what needed to be tightened up, make the edits, and move on. Boom, boom, boom. But lately? I'll sit there staring at the same paragraph for twenty minutes. I'll read a sentence, and it's like the words just kind of float there, and it takes me twice as long to process what it actually means in the context of the whole proposal. And then when I go to rewrite it, I just... I get stuck. I second-guess every little word choice. Is "indicate" better than "demonstrate"? Does this sentence flow into the next one properly? I'll rewrite the same sentence four times and still not be sure if it's right. 

And it's not just at work, either. It bleeds into everything. Even something stupidly simple, like picking out materials for a home repair. The other week, I noticed the weatherstripping on the back door was peeling off, so I went to the hardware store to get a replacement. I stood in that aisle for what felt like an eternity. There were, like, three options—foam, rubber, vinyl—and I just stood there, paralyzed, trying to weigh the pros and cons of each one in my head, and my brain just felt so incredibly slow and foggy. I couldn't just make a decision. I kept going back and forth, second-guessing myself over a ten-dollar roll of tape. I ended up leaving without buying anything because it was just too much mental effort. 

So, yeah, my thinking is definitely slower. It takes me so much longer to process information and make even the smallest decisions because my mind just feels... clouded, I guess. It’s really frustrating, especially because I rely on my brain so much for my job. It’s like the processor is just running on a fraction of its normal speed.
